# Managing a project

For a project kx already knows. `kx-cli` is the reference for every command and
its `--json`; this is which one answers which question, and where to stop.

## Where this stops

**Nothing here touches 1Password.** `op` authorises through the desktop app,
which a headless machine does not have, so every command that reads or writes
the vault has nowhere to get an answer from: `kx creds`, `kx exec`, `kx open`,
and the credential stages of `kx doctor`.

What is left is the whole model — which services a project uses, which
variables it needs — and that is most of the work. Do it, and hand the vault
half to a person with the exact command.

### What you can and cannot say about credentials

You can say what a project **needs**: `kx creds --project <id> --json` returns
`required`, derived from the model and needing no vault at all.

You cannot say what is **missing**. That is a comparison against the item, and
the item cannot be read here. When `readFailure` is set, `missing`, `unfilled`
and `extra` come back **empty because nothing was compared — not because
nothing is missing**. Reporting those empty lists as "nothing is missing" tells
someone their vault is complete when it may hold nothing at all.

The same trap in `kx doctor --json`: its `credentials` block is empty for the
same reason, and its `checks` that failed here failed on missing CLIs, not on
credentials. `blocked` is the honest number — the checks that could not run.

So the sentence to hand back is "this project requires these N credentials;
whether they are filled in is unknown from here", never "these are missing".

| Asked | Run |
|---|---|
| what does this project use | `kx connector list --json` |
| what does the code look like it uses | `kx connector suggest` |
| start using a service | `kx connector add <id>` |
| keep separate keys per environment for one | `kx connector add <id> --per-environment <field>` — the project's choice, recorded on its connection |
| stop using one | `kx connector remove <id>` |
| the app needs a new variable | `kx env add <NAME> --secret` |
| what does it declare already | `kx env list --json` |
| what credentials does it require | `kx creds --project <id> --json` → `required` only |

After any change: **`kx sync`**. `projects.json` alone changes nothing in the
repository.

## Two rules worth knowing before you change anything

**`projects.json` is shared.** Adding or removing a connector applies to every
branch of every checkout, immediately, for everyone. There is no per-branch
setting. `kx-cli` has what that means at merge time.

**`op run` is all or nothing.** One reference it cannot resolve fails the whole
command, not just that variable — so a connector added before its credential
exists turns every `kx exec` for whoever syncs next into a question: launch
without it? (`kx-cli` says how that question is answered, and when
`--skip-missing` is the answer.) That is the reason to say, every time you add
one, that a credential is now owed and by whom.

## Removing a service

The one to slow down for. It is global, and the intent is usually local — the
branch in front of you. `kx connector remove` greps the working tree for the
connector's variables first and shows what it found; read that before
answering, because another branch may still need them.

Nothing is deleted from the vault, and you could not delete it from here
anyway. The fields stop being required, which makes them *extra*: reported,
and removed only when somebody with 1Password says so.

## What you cannot do, and must not pretend to

**Fill a credential, check one, or run anything through `op`.** Not a
restriction to work around — there is no authorisation available here.

**Report a project as working.** You can say its model is complete. Whether
the credentials work is `kx doctor` on a machine that has 1Password, and until
someone runs it the answer is unknown rather than good.

**Read or write a secret anywhere.** Values live in 1Password. Nothing kx
prints contains one, and nothing you write should.

**Migrate a repository's `.env` files.** `kx env migrate` writes to the vault
and asks a question per variable, neither of which is available here. Say the
repository has them and that the command is `kx env migrate`, run by a person
in that checkout.

**File an issue on kx.** `kx report` publishes, and `--yes` is what skips the
one moment a human looks at the redacted body before it becomes public. Write
the report out for someone to paste; do not send it. It redacts and cleans
what it is given, but that is a last line, not permission to skip the first.
